items.title: Step two threads yourself
items.blurb: Pick the next line for each thread yourself, or let a random schedule do it. Shared memory is in the middle.
items.notes: Visibility, atomicity and ordering are three separate failures. `count++` is three steps, so it needs atomicity (a lock or an atomic). Double-checked locking needs ordering: without `volatile` the write of `instance` may become visible before the constructor's writes. A plain stop flag needs visibility: nothing forces the loop to re-read it.
items.lessonTitle: Java concurrency and the memory model
challenges: Lose an increment: get count to finish below 4 with a plain int
Catch double-checked locking handing out a half-built object
Fix the counter with synchronized or AtomicInteger and run it to 4

items.title: Size a ThreadPoolExecutor
items.blurb: Tasks arrive steadily, then four times as fast for ten seconds. Change the pool and its queue and watch threads, queue and latency.
items.notes: The executor queues first and grows second, so with an unbounded queue `maximumPoolSize` is dead config and the queue absorbs the overload as latency. Bound the queue, pick a rejection policy on purpose, and treat CallerRunsPolicy as back-pressure: the submitter slows down.
items.lessonTitle: Java concurrency and the memory model
challenges: With the unbounded queue, see that the pool never grows past core
Make the pool grow beyond core (it needs a bounded queue)
Use CallerRunsPolicy to push back instead of rejecting

items.title: Threads, processes and asyncio on the same work
items.blurb: Each row is one task over time: running, waiting for the GIL, waiting on I/O, or queued.
items.notes: The GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so threads overlap waiting, not computing. CPU-bound work needs processes (or a free-threaded build), at the cost of start-up and pickling. asyncio overlaps I/O on one thread, but a coroutine that computes holds everyone else up.
items.lessonTitle: How Python runs - the GIL, asyncio and memory
challenges: Run the CPU-bound work on threads and see almost no speed-up
Get at least a 3× speed-up on the CPU-bound work
Show that threads are fine for I/O-bound work

items.title: One blocking call on the event loop
items.blurb: An asyncio service gets a request every 40 ms. At one second, one handler does something slow. Watch everyone else.
items.notes: The loop is a single thread: a synchronous call inside a coroutine blocks every request, not just its own. Await non-blocking versions, or offload blocking and CPU work with `asyncio.to_thread` or a process pool.
items.lessonTitle: How Python runs - the GIL, asyncio and memory
challenges: Freeze the service with a blocking call
Do the same slow work without hurting anyone else

items.title: A CPU scheduler
items.blurb: Choose a workload and a policy. Each bar is one job; green is running, red is ready but waiting. Add a context-switch cost to see what preemption costs.
items.notes: No policy wins everything. SRTF minimises waiting but needs to know the future; round robin gives good response time at the cost of switches; MLFQ learns which jobs are short by watching them. Real schedulers blend fairness, priorities and cache affinity.
items.lessonTitle: Processes, threads and CPU scheduling
challenges: See the convoy effect: average wait above 15 ms under FCFS
Get the average wait under 4 ms on the convoy workload
Make round robin spend over 20% of the CPU on context switches

items.title: Page replacement
items.blurb: Feed a reference string to a replacement policy. Each column is one memory reference; each row is a physical frame. F marks a page fault.
items.notes: Optimal is the floor no real policy reaches. LRU approximates it when the past predicts the future, Clock approximates LRU cheaply, and FIFO can get worse with more memory. A loop just bigger than memory is LRU's worst case.
items.lessonTitle: Virtual memory and paging
challenges: Find Belady's anomaly: one more frame, more faults
Make LRU fault on every single reference
Find a frame count where LRU matches the optimal policy on the textbook string

items.title: Dining philosophers
items.blurb: Philosophers sit around a table with one fork between each pair and need both neighbouring forks to eat. Each strategy runs 100 times with random timing.
items.notes: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions. A global lock order removes circular wait, tryLock with back-off removes hold-and-wait, and limiting the number of contenders makes a full cycle impossible. Shorter thinking times mean more contention and faster deadlocks.
items.lessonTitle: Synchronisation: mutexes, semaphores, monitors and deadlock
challenges: Deadlock the table
Break circular wait with a lock order and never deadlock
Prevent deadlock with a semaphore instead

items.title: PID 1, signals and zombies in a container
items.blurb: Choose how the container starts, then stop it, or make the app leave an orphan behind.
items.notes: PID 1 must forward signals and reap orphans, and the kernel gives it no default signal actions. Use exec-form CMD with a SIGTERM handler, or `docker run --init` (tini) to get both jobs done for you.
items.lessonTitle: Linux processes, memory and files
challenges: Stop the container and lose in-flight requests to SIGKILL
Make a zombie that PID 1 never reaps
Find a setup that stops cleanly (exit 0)

items.title: A JVM inside a 2 GiB pod
items.blurb: The bar is the process's memory against the cgroup limit (the red line).
items.notes: Heap is only part of a JVM's footprint: metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers and the code cache all count against the cgroup. Size the heap as a percentage of the limit (`MaxRAMPercentage` around 70-75%) and leave room for the rest.
items.lessonTitle: Linux processes, memory and files
challenges: Get the pod OOMKilled at full load
Size the heap so it survives full load with at least 100 MiB to spare

items.title: A descriptor leak
items.blurb: A few requests forget to close a socket. Watch the open descriptor count against `ulimit -n`.
items.notes: A climbing count is a leak; a high flat one is a limit to raise. Raising the limit on a leak only moves the outage.
items.lessonTitle: Linux processes, memory and files
challenges: See the process hit the limit within half an hour
Fix it so the count stays flat

items.title: Slow start, round by round
items.blurb: How many round trips does a response take on a new connection?
items.notes: Most web responses are latency-bound: a new TCP connection needs handshakes plus several slow-start round trips. Keep-alive and connection pooling are the cheapest speed-up there is.
items.lessonTitle: What happens on the wire - DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP
challenges: Download 500 KB on a new connection
Make the same download faster without changing the size

items.title: One lost packet, three protocols
items.blurb: A page of small resources over a lossy link. Bars are when each resource finished; amber ones were held up by a loss.
items.notes: HTTP/2 fixed HTTP/1.1's queueing with streams, but on one TCP connection a lost packet still blocks everything behind it. QUIC moves loss recovery into each stream, and does the handshake in one round trip.
items.lessonTitle: What happens on the wire - DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP
challenges: Lose packets on HTTP/2 and see more resources delayed than packets lost
Try the same loss on HTTP/3

items.title: Joins on two tiny tables
items.blurb: Users and orders. Dee has no orders, Cy has only a refunded one, and order 105 was a guest checkout with no user. Change the join, where the filter goes, and how you count.
items.notes: ON decides which rows match; WHERE filters the joined result afterwards. A condition on the right-hand table belongs in ON if you want to keep unmatched left rows. And COUNT(*) counts rows, including the NULL-filled ones an outer join adds, while COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values.
items.lessonTitle: SQL queries: joins, NULLs and grouping
challenges: List every user, including those with no orders
Turn a LEFT JOIN back into an inner join with a WHERE clause
Find the users with no paid order (Cy and Dee)
Watch COUNT(*) claim Dee has an order

items.title: Window functions on eight sales
items.blurb: Each row is one month's sale for a rep in North or South. Note the ties: two North sales of 120 and three South sales of 80.
items.notes: ROW_NUMBER is unique, RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK doesn't. Filter on a window function from an outer query or CTE, because WHERE runs first. And with ORDER BY but no frame, aggregates use RANGE … CURRENT ROW, which includes every tied row; say ROWS when you mean physical rows.
items.lessonTitle: SQL analytics: window functions, CTEs and query plans
challenges: Find a RANK() that skips a number after a tie
Return the top two sales in each region
Make two rows share one running total, then fix it with a ROWS frame

items.title: Two sessions, one row
items.blurb: Run statements in two sessions, one at a time. The table shows every row version and which session can see it.
items.notes: An UPDATE writes a new row version; readers keep seeing the version their snapshot allows, so they never block writers. A lost update comes from reading in one statement and writing what you read in another: use `SET balance = balance + 10`, `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, or REPEATABLE READ with a retry.
items.lessonTitle: Postgres internals - MVCC, isolation, locks and vacuum
challenges: Lose an update: two +10s that leave the balance at 110
Get REPEATABLE READ to refuse a concurrent update
Run VACUUM and watch dead versions go

items.title: The migration that queued every query
items.blurb: A report query is running when a migration asks for an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.
items.notes: Lock requests queue in order, so an ALTER waiting behind one long query blocks every query that arrives after it. Use `lock_timeout` (and retries) on migrations, and keep long transactions off the primary.
items.lessonTitle: Postgres internals - MVCC, isolation, locks and vacuum
challenges: Watch the connection pool fill up behind the ALTER
Set a lock_timeout short enough that no request fails

items.title: A JWT verifier, one check at a time
items.blurb: Pick a token an attacker might send, and the checks your verifier makes. The server issues RS256 tokens for the audience "api".
items.notes: Verify the signature with a pinned algorithm and a trusted key, then check exp, iss and aud. Each missing check is one specific attack that works. Use a maintained library and configure it explicitly rather than trusting the token's header.
items.lessonTitle: Authentication, sessions and authorisation
challenges: Get a forged admin token accepted
Make "alg: none" work against a server that does verify signatures
Find checks that reject every attack and still accept the genuine token

items.title: OAuth flows under attack
items.blurb: Pick a flow and an attack, and decide whether the client sends state and whether the authorization server matches redirect URIs exactly.
items.notes: Authorization code with PKCE for every client, exact redirect URI matching on the server, and state (or PKCE) against login CSRF. The implicit flow puts tokens in URLs, where history, logs and other scripts can read them; it is retired.
items.lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
challenges: Steal an access token from the implicit flow
Find the attack that PKCE alone does not stop
Configure a public client that blocks all four attacks

items.title: Six attacks against your defences
items.blurb: Turn defences on and see which attacks still land. Pick an attack to see its steps.
items.notes: Each attack has a defence at its root: escaping for XSS, SameSite and tokens for CSRF, parameters for SQL injection, egress control for SSRF, per-object checks for access control, an exact allow list for CORS. Measures like HttpOnly, UUIDs and IMDSv2 limit damage; they are layers, not fixes.
items.lessonTitle: Web attacks and their defences
challenges: Stop the stored XSS with a single defence
See HttpOnly limit an XSS without stopping it
Block all six attacks with only five defences

items.title: Requests, limits and QoS on three nodes
items.blurb: web is a latency-sensitive service; batch pods run with no requests at all.
items.notes: Requests decide placement, limits decide what happens at runtime. Under memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable ones using more than they asked for. A CPU limit shows up as latency, not errors.
items.lessonTitle: Containers and Kubernetes
challenges: Leave a pod Pending
Get a web pod CPU-throttled
Get pods evicted under memory pressure

items.title: The reconcile loop and a rollout
items.blurb: A Deployment of four pods. Delete pods, push images and watch the controller close the gap.
items.notes: Controllers don't follow scripts; they compare desired and actual state on every pass. A rollout with maxUnavailable 0 removes old pods only after new ones are Ready, so a broken image stalls instead of taking the service down, as long as readiness actually means ready.
items.lessonTitle: Containers and Kubernetes
challenges: Delete a pod and watch it come back
Push a broken image and see the rollout stall in CrashLoopBackOff
Recover with kubectl rollout undo

items.title: How AWS decides
items.blurb: Pick a request and the policies in play. The trail says which rule decided.
items.notes: Explicit Deny always wins; without an Allow the answer is Deny. Boundaries and SCPs never grant anything, they only cap what policies can grant.
items.lessonTitle: Cloud building blocks on AWS
challenges: See an explicit Deny beat an Allow
Hit an implicit deny
See a permissions boundary cap an identity policy

items.title: Follow a packet through the VPC
items.blurb: Five flows: three should work and two should be blocked. Break things and see exactly where each packet stops.
items.notes: Public subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway; private ones route it to a NAT gateway in a public subnet. Security groups reference each other (app allows the load balancer's group, the database allows the app's), so nothing is open to the world except the load balancer.
items.lessonTitle: Cloud building blocks on AWS
challenges: Break outbound calls from the private subnet
Expose something to the internet that shouldn't be
Get all five flows right again

items.title: A bad build under each strategy
items.blurb: The new build fails some requests. Compare how much traffic sees it and how many requests fail.
items.notes: Every strategy runs two versions for a while; what differs is how many users meet a bad one and how fast you can undo it. Canaries need automated analysis to be worth it; feature flags turn off in seconds.
items.lessonTitle: CI/CD, deployment strategies and infrastructure as code
challenges: Get more than half the traffic onto the bad build
Keep failed requests under 50

items.title: Rename a column without downtime
items.blurb: Rename users.fullname to full_name while the app keeps serving traffic. Pick the steps in order.
items.notes: Expand (add the new column, write both, backfill), switch reads, then contract (drop the old one), each step deployed on its own. Every step must work with both app versions that run during it.
items.lessonTitle: CI/CD, deployment strategies and infrastructure as code
challenges: Rename it in one step and break the running version
Finish the rename with no step breaking either version

items.title: The broken commit that kept coming back
items.blurb: Thirty minutes of the box's deploy timer after a commit that crashes on start.
items.notes: Automatic recovery that repeats the failure is a retry storm. Remember what failed and stop retrying it until something changes.
items.lessonTitle: Case study: your own box
challenges: See the site flap while the broken commit is retried
Stop the retry storm

items.title: A day on an 8 GB box
items.blurb: Agent sessions open through the day, work for a while, then sit idle. At 18:00 a batch of sessions opens at once.
items.notes: The scarcer the resource, the less you keep around, with a bound on how much you do at once and a pass frequent enough to catch demand that grows between runs.
items.lessonTitle: Case study: your own box
challenges: Run out of memory with the fixed rule
Survive the day

items.title: Four test shapes, one flawed service
items.blurb: The service has three planted flaws. Run each kind of test and see which flaws it exposes. (Turn a flaw off to see a clean run.)
items.notes: A passing load test says only that this shape of traffic works. Stress tests find ceilings and bottlenecks, spike tests find slow scaling, and only a long soak finds leaks. Pick the shapes that match the risks you have.
items.lessonTitle: Testing strategy: from unit tests to chaos
challenges: Pass a load test even though all three flaws are present
Find the memory leak
Find all three planted flaws

items.title: Where the time and money go in one call
items.blurb: Count tokens in a few kinds of text, then change the prompt, the output and caching and watch the timeline.
items.notes: Latency is roughly time to first token plus output tokens divided by decode speed, so output length is the big lever. Caching a stable prefix cuts prefill time and input cost; streaming changes when words appear, not when the answer is done.
items.lessonTitle: How LLMs behave - tokens, context and sampling
challenges: Make a call take over 10 seconds with a short prompt
Get the first words on screen within half a second of a long call
Cut the time to first token with prompt caching

items.title: Temperature, top-k and top-p on one distribution
items.blurb: The bars are the probabilities of the next token. Change the settings, then sample twenty times.
items.notes: Temperature reshapes the whole distribution; top-k and top-p remove its tail. Use a low temperature where there's one right answer (labels, extraction, code) and more where variety is the point.
items.lessonTitle: How LLMs behave - tokens, context and sampling
challenges: Get twenty different-looking cat names
Get the same label twenty times out of twenty

items.title: Getting JSON you can trust
items.blurb: Two thousand records extracted by a model. Change how you ask for JSON and what you do with the answer.
items.notes: Ask for structure (JSON mode or, better, schema-constrained decoding), validate in code anyway, and retry with the validation error. Constrained decoding fixes the format, not the content, and it can't fix a response cut off by max_tokens.
items.lessonTitle: Prompting, structured output and tool calls
challenges: Let bad records through by not validating
Get to 99.5% valid records

items.title: One round of tool use, message by message
items.blurb: The model asks for get_weather. Choose what your app does with the request, and see the messages that follow.
items.notes: The model only asks; your code validates, runs and answers every tool request, matching ids, before anything else. Return failures as errors the model can act on, and treat tool results as untrusted text.
items.lessonTitle: Prompting, structured output and tool calls
challenges: Complete the round properly
Break the conversation by not returning a tool result
See a tool result hijack the answer

items.title: Searching a layered graph
items.blurb: 400 vectors, flattened to two dimensions so you can see them. The search starts in the sparse top layer and greedily works down.
items.notes: Approximate search trades a little recall for a lot of speed, and ef_search is the dial at query time. Exact search is fine until it isn't: at millions of vectors you need an index, and you should measure its recall.
items.lessonTitle: Embeddings and vector search
challenges: Find a query or setting where recall@10 drops below 100%
Get every true neighbour (100% recall) while computing fewer than a third of the distances

items.title: Keywords, vectors, and both
items.blurb: Four help-centre queries, each with one right page. Try each search method on each query.
items.notes: Embeddings match meaning and blur exact tokens; BM25 matches tokens and misses paraphrase. Fuse both (reciprocal rank fusion is simple and robust), then re-rank the top few dozen.
items.lessonTitle: Embeddings and vector search
challenges: Find a query that vector search gets wrong
Get all four right

items.title: Seven questions, seven ways to fail
items.blurb: A support bot over a help centre. Each question breaks at a different stage of the pipeline until you add the piece it needs.
items.notes: Quality comes from retrieval more than from the prompt: chunking, freshness, query rewriting, hybrid search, permission filters, re-ranking, then a grounded prompt that can say "I don't know". Diagnose a bad answer to the stage that caused it.
items.lessonTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation
challenges: Find the data leak and stop it
Answer all seven well
Answer all seven with under 4,000 tokens of context

items.title: Is that 2-point drop real?
items.blurb: A cheaper model is truly 2 points worse. How often would your eval notice?
items.notes: An eval is a sample, so its score has error bars. Compare models on the same cases (paired), report intervals, and size the set for the smallest difference you care about.
items.lessonTitle: Evals - measuring LLM quality
challenges: See the cheaper model look as good in over 20% of runs
Make the 2-point difference clearly measurable

items.title: A thousand runs of the same task
items.blurb: A task needs a few tool calls; some calls fail and an agent wastes some steps. Compare structures and controls.
items.notes: Use the simplest structure that works: a workflow when the steps are known, an agent when they aren't. Give agents budgets, return tool errors as information, and keep context bounded, because cost grows with every step.
items.lessonTitle: Agents - tool loops, planning and control
challenges: Watch runs crash when tool errors aren't returned to the model
Get an agent to finish 95% of tasks
Do it cheaper with a fixed workflow

items.title: An MCP session, message by message
items.blurb: Step through a session between a host and a GitHub server, over either transport. Then switch to the attacks and see which defences stop each one.
items.notes: The protocol is small: initialise and agree capabilities, list, call, get told about changes. What matters in production is around it: the transport and its authorisation, and treating every description and result a server sends as untrusted input.
items.lessonTitle: MCP servers - one tool interface for every model
challenges: Step through a whole session, from initialize to a tool result
Compare the two transports
Stop every attack

items.title: One agent or many
items.blurb: A research task with some number of sub-questions. Compare one agent working through them in one context, a fixed fan-out workflow, and an orchestrator with worker agents.
items.notes: Multi-agent designs pay off for broad, independent work: fresh contexts keep quality up as breadth grows, and parallelism keeps wall time flat. They cost several times the tokens, and they hurt when sub-tasks share decisions that workers can't see.
items.lessonTitle: Multi-agent systems and agent memory
challenges: Find a task where the orchestrator gives the best quality
Find a task where splitting makes quality worse than one agent

items.title: What a crash costs an agent run
items.blurb: An eight-step report workflow: plan, three research steps, draft, wait for human approval, email the client, log it in the CRM. Pick how the run is executed and what goes wrong.
items.notes: Checkpointing after each step saves the work, but a step that crashed after acting will act again. Record side effects with idempotency keys, and keep pending human approvals in durable state, so a restart replays history instead of repeating the world.
items.lessonTitle: Durable orchestration, reflection and autonomy levels
challenges: Send the client the report twice
Survive a deploy during the approval wait without asking the approver again
Crash right after the email is sent, and still send exactly one

items.title: Cutting the monthly bill
items.blurb: The lesson's feature: 200,000 requests a day at 3,000 tokens in and 300 out.
items.notes: Caching a stable prefix, routing easy requests to a small model, capping output and batching offline work each compound. Do the arithmetic per request before choosing a model.
items.lessonTitle: Serving LLMs - latency, cost and reliability
challenges: Cut the bill by half
Cut it by 80%

items.title: What fits on a GPU
items.blurb: Self-host a model on 80 GB GPUs: weights, KV cache, batching and load.
items.notes: Weights decide whether it fits; the KV cache decides how many conversations run at once; memory bandwidth decides tokens per second. Continuous batching and quantisation are why self-hosting can pay, at enough volume.
items.lessonTitle: Serving LLMs - latency, cost and reliability
challenges: Find a model that doesn't fit at all
Serve the 70B model to 4 requests a second with first tokens under 2 s

items.title: Assume the model is fooled
items.blurb: An assistant with email, browsing and file tools meets six attacks. The model follows every one of them; your design decides what happens next.
items.notes: Prompt injection can't be fully prevented, so design for a model that will sometimes be fooled: least privilege, allowlists, human confirmation for irreversible actions, and no untrusted way out (links, images, emails).
items.lessonTitle: Safety, prompt injection and guardrails
challenges: Stop every attack
Stop every attack with little friction

items.title: Precision, recall and when to stay quiet
items.blurb: Each candidate comment gets a confidence score. Choose where the bot starts posting.
items.notes: A reviewer that cries wolf gets muted, so favour precision and post less. Measure it on historical PRs, then online through how often developers act on or dismiss comments.
items.lessonTitle: AI system design: a pull-request review assistant
challenges: Keep precision at 70% or more
Catch half the real issues with precision still at 70%+
